results.summary: This design generates and plays a maze game, using Ellers algorithm to create mazes of arbitrary size up to a constraint. It outputs a VGA signal and reads input from a PMOD gamepad, allowing a user to navigate the maze. The full-featured version includes the maze generator in RTL, while smaller tile configurations omit the generator due to area restrictions. Testing is done via a VGA playground or basic simulations, and it requires a PMOD Gamepad and PMOD VGA for interactive use.

This project is an analog MCML VCO core intended for a future PLL. The documentation consists only of placeholder text, providing no details on how the circuit works or how to test it. No external hardware is listed, and the design is marked as analog with two analog pins. Because the documentation is essentially empty, little can be said about its operation or verification.

This design produces a deep-space nebula effect based on Sierpinski fractal logic, along with 4-voice PWM chiptune audio. It outputs VGA video and PWM audio, with inputs controlling speed and density. The documentation is placeholder text, so the exact implementation and testing procedure are not described. It requires a VGA PMOD for display and likely a speaker or audio output for the PWM signal.

This design implements a spiking neural network tile with four Leaky Integrate-and-Fire neurons arranged in a 2x2 grid. A single microcode-driven compute worker processes spike events in round-robin order, and the tile supports configuration via weight and ISA headers. Inputs and outputs include spike signals, weight data, and handshake lines for tile-to-tile communication. The documentation is brief but indicates a configurable neural network accelerator with a custom instruction set.

This design implements a 4-bit bidirectional universal shift register compatible with the SN74LS194A. It supports hold, shift right, shift left, and parallel load modes, with asynchronous active-low clear. The design is clocked on the rising edge and uses mode select pins S1 and S0 to choose the operation. No external hardware is required, though switches and LEDs on a demo board can be used for testing.

This is an 8-bit, 2-stage pipelined CPU with a custom ISA inspired by ARM, featuring four registers and thirteen instructions. It interfaces with an external byte-addressable 8-bit SRAM that must provide combinational read and a write enable signal. The CPU uses dedicated input, output, and bidirectional pins for data, address, and control signals. The design requires an external SRAM chip to function and is intended for embedded processing tasks.

This project is a small demoscene-style VGA generator that produces a 640x480 @ 60Hz video signal with an animated XOR background and a central logo inspired by the Tiny Tapeout mark. The image is computed entirely in hardware using combinational logic, without a frame buffer or external memory. Two input pins allow inverting colors and freezing the logo at the center. It requires a VGA PMOD for video output and is tested by connecting it to a Tiny Tapeout demo board.

This is a custom 4-bit RISC microprocessor designed for Tiny Tapeout. It uses external ROM for instructions and external RAM for data, with dedicated address and data pins for each. The documentation is minimal, stating only that instructions are executed, and promises future updates with ISA details. External RAM and ROM chips are required, likely emulated by a microcontroller.

This design converts an 8-bit binary number to a decimal number displayed as three BCD digits on a 7-segment display, using the Double Dabble algorithm. The conversion is implemented with combinational logic, while a state machine sequentially displays hundreds, tens, ones, and a decimal point. The design has an 8-bit binary input, an 8-bit output for the 7-segment display, and an 8-bit bidirectional port that outputs the tens and ones. It requires no external hardware and has been tested with several binary values.

This project implements the SIMON64/128 block cipher with an SPI interface for communication. It provides busy and output valid signals, and can be controlled via SPI from a microcontroller or PC. Automated tests using cocotb and pytest are included, and the design can be used with MicroPython on a Tiny Tapeout demo board or an external FTDI breakout. The documentation covers parts of the cipher and testing but leaves out full details.
